title: Responses API shim: interop mapping and migration plan
creator: Asha Patel
description: Goal: deliver a compatibility shim and migration guidance so Redwood customers using the OpenAI Responses API can switch to Redwood with minimal code changes. Focus areas: streaming delta parity, function/tool calling semantics, structured output (JSON/schema enforcement), and error/metadata mapping. This ticket owns the design, prototype, and rollout plan for the shim (server-side translation layer + SDK helpers + tests).
background: Customers and partner integrations expect OpenAI Responses semantics (message framing, 'tool' calling flow, JSON structured responses, and streaming deltas). Redwood's native API historically used chat/generation endpoints with different event shapes and a richer runtime model (fallbacks, model variants, batch prefixes, and explicit runtime metadata). Previous analysis (ENG-8342) enumerated gaps; this ticket converts that analysis into an actionable design and implementation plan that minimizes risk to runtime SLOs.
scope: In-scope: request/response mapping for the Responses surface (both sync and streaming), function/tool calling protocol translation, structured output validation helpers, SDK sugar for migration, comprehensive unit/integration tests, telemetry mappings for usage/latency/cost, and rollout controls (feature flag + gradual ramp). Out-of-scope: changing underlying runtime kernels or adding new model capabilities beyond conservative fallbacks.
non_goals: Support every historical OpenAI edge case (we will prioritize common usage patterns)
compatibility_gaps_summary: Streaming event shapes differ: OpenAI Responses uses named delta fragments with top-level 'type' tags (message.delta, tool.progress, tool.result). Redwood streams token deltas and structured chunks that include runtime metadata in separate envelopes.

Function/tool calling state machine: OpenAI expects explicit 'call' -> 'tool_exec' -> 'return' lifecycle; Redwood's tool integrations are event-driven with autoscheduling and partial KV cache exposures.
Structured JSON enforcement: OpenAI provides schema-like validation and explicit 'parse' errors; Redwood returns structured candidates but does not reject non-conforming tokens by default.
Error and usage metadata naming: usage fields, error codes, and content policy labels use different keys and shapes.
Attachment/streamed binary payloads: OpenAI may include non-text tool outputs in streaming events; Redwood currently streams text-first with optional artifact URLs post-response.
Stop sequence and truncation semantics differ slightly under high-concurrency batching.
technical_approach: Implement a stateless shim layer at the API ingress that accepts OpenAI Responses requests and emits Redwood-native requests to the runtime, and vice-versa for responses.
Streaming translation: convert Redwood streaming tokens into OpenAI-style delta envelopes. Maintain event ordering and include a 'meta' delta with usage/partial-ids at stream end.

Function calling semantics: introduce a slim state machine inside the shim that maps OpenAI 'call' decisions to Redwood tool invocation API. Provide auto-retry for transient tool failures and explicit 'tool_result' event mapping.

Structured output: integrate a lightweight validation step post-generation to detect JSON/schema mismatches. If mismatch -> emit an OpenAI-compatible 'parse_error' event and include candidate text and diagnostics.
Errors & rate limits: normalize runtime errors to OpenAI-style error objects and map rate-limit headers. Add headers for Redwood-specific fallbacks used during canary phases.
SDK helpers: add 'responses_compat' flag in Redwood SDKs that toggles request shaping (message -> input mapping) and response parsing helpers for tools, streaming, and schema validation.
Telemetry: emit translation-layer metrics (latency delta, conversion errors, tool invocation counts) to the platform's observability pipeline. Tag metrics with 'compat=responses' and 'shim_version'.
Rollout: behind feature-flag per-tenant with gradual ramp and automatic rollback on error-rate/latency regressions.
acceptance_criteria: Shim accepts canonical OpenAI Responses requests and returns equivalent OpenAI-shaped responses for 95% of top-100 customer prompts (see sample set)
Streaming delta tests pass end-to-end: client receives valid sequence of message.delta/tool.progress/tool.result events in expected order
Function calling critical flows (call-with-args -> tool invocation -> tool_result) validated with three real tools (search, calculator, file-retriever)
Structured output validation triggers parse_error correctly and attached diagnostics include raw model output and validation diff
Performance: shim adds <10ms median tail (p50/p95) for non-streaming requests; streaming throughput benchmarks within 5% of baseline
Telemetry and logs surface mapping failures and per-tenant rollback triggers
SDK compatibility helpers published with examples and migration guide
detailed_tasks: T1: Design shim protocol and event mapping spec (doc + canonical examples)
T2: Implement shim ingress/egress translator (Go service behind API gateway)
T3: Streaming translation engine with ordering guarantees and backpressure handling
T4: Tool calling state machine and tool invocation adapter (retries, timeouts)
T5: Structured-output validator module and error envelope generator
T6: SDK changes: responses_compat flag + helpers for streaming parsing and tool flow
T7: Unit tests: mapping coverage + fuzzing of malformed events
T8: Integration tests: e2e against runtime with synthetic tools and real sample prompts
T9: Performance tests and canary harness
T10: Documentation: migration guide, examples, known-issues
T11: Rollout orchestration: feature flagging, alerts, rollback playbook
progress_updates: 2026-03-02: Kickoff meeting with Runtime, SDK, and Observability teams. Agreed to implement shim as a separate service to avoid touching critical runtime paths. (Asha)

2026-03-05: Drafted event mapping spec (alpha). Focused on mapping token-level deltas to 'message.delta' envelopes and adding a 'meta' end-of-stream event with usage metadata. Request review by Marcus and Elena. (Asha)
2026-03-08: Prototype streaming translator implemented (PoC) that converts existing Redwood stream into SSE with OpenAI envelope shape. P50 added ~6ms latency in internal bench. (Marcus)
2026-03-10: Spike for function calling adapter completed: validated mapping for call->tool_result using the search tool. Need robust retry semantics for tool timeouts. (Marcus)

2026-03-12: Added structured-output validator prototype using JSON schema; discovered failure mode when model emits trailing commas — plan to implement tolerant parser and provide diagnostics. (Elena)
Blocking: need QA test tooling to inject large streaming tool_result payloads; infra tickets opened.
decisions: Shim will be stateless between request/response and use external state storage only for long-running tool invocations (>30s).
We will not change Redwood's runtime event format; translator will live in the API tier to keep runtime stable.
Structured-output validator will favor non-destructive diagnostics: do not mutate model output unless explicitly opted-in by tenant.
risks_mitigation: Risk: shim introduces latency — mitigate by optimizing critical path in Go and benchmarking with workload generator
Risk: function calling mismatches cause silent failures — mitigate by end-to-end tests with canary tenants and strict telemetry alerting
Risk: schema validation creates false-positives on near-JSON outputs — mitigate with tolerant parser and sample-driven tuning
notes_for_QA: Test streaming against both long-running and short responses
Validate tool-calling flows with injected tool slowdowns and error codes
Run structured-output fuzzing with 500+ schemas from sample corpus
Verify telemetry tags (compat=responses, shim_version) are present
